title: A Predictive Framework for Identifying Fake Reviews on E-Commerce Platforms
affiliations: Bangladesh University of Business and Technology, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Jahangirnagar University and Bangladesh University of Business and Technology

detail.title: A Predictive Framework for Identifying Fake Reviews on E-Commerce Platforms
detail.abstract: Fake reviews in particular are degrading the trust between e-commerce and consumers, because theycan mislead them and misrepresent about the products. To determine this, we propose a hybrid fakereview detection framework with both the linguistic and behavioural signals. A distilled transformerencoder produces first-order rich-bidirectional contextual representations of each review so as tocapture subtle semantic irregularities. These embeddings are then analyzed by a bidirectional LSTMin order to understand long-range sequential dependencies and an attention mechanism is used tohighlight the most deception-worthy words and phrases. In parallel, teaching behaviour features at ascale that is representative of the structure of reviews and statistics of the scripts are fused with deeptextual representation, allowing the model to make use of stylistic anomalies alongside the extractionof contextual meaning, making far more reliable authenticity prediction possible. The experiments onthe Amazon Enhanced Fake Reviews Dataset show the proposed model has an accuracy of 99.85%,99.87% precision, 99.84% recall, and a 99.85% F1-score, which is evenly better than strong baselineproposals. These results validate that the joint utilization of transformer-level semantics, sequentialdynamics, attention-guided saliency, and behavioral evidence is a highly reliable solution to detectfraudulent opinion spam, hence the introduced framework is ready to be used in practice in real onlinemarketplaces for preserving the authenticity of reviews and protecting consumers from misleadingcontents.

title: Predictive Analytics for Customer Purchase Behavior Using Machine Learning in ECommerce
affiliations: Ladoke Akintola University of Technology and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Predictive Analytics for Customer Purchase Behavior Using Machine Learning in ECommerce
detail.abstract: The continued expansion of e-commerce has made accurate prediction of customer purchase behavior a critical capability for achieving competitive advantage and operational efficiency. While traditional rule-based systems and descriptive analytics have been widely adopted, they are limited in their ability to capture complex, non-linear, and evolving customer decision processes. This study proposes a machine learning– driven predictive analytics framework for modeling customer purchase intention and behavior in modern ecommerce environments. The framework leverages multi-source data, including transactional records, browsing behavior, and contextual attributes, and applies supervised and ensemble learning techniques to identify patterns indicative of purchasing outcomes. A systematic evaluation strategy is employed using standard performance metrics and comparative analysis against conventional analytical approaches. The results demonstrate notable improvements in prediction accuracy, more precise customer targeting, and enhanced decision support for marketing and demand planning activities. Furthermore, the proposed approach enables scalable and adaptive modeling of customer behavior, addressing key limitations associated with static analytical methods. The study contributes to the development of intelligent e-commerce systems by providing a practical predictive framework that enhances personalization and strategic decision-making. From a theoretical perspective, the findings reinforce the effectiveness of data-driven learning paradigms for capturing complex consumer behavior in large-scale digital commerce settings.

title: Gone with the Wind? Climate Shocks, Insurance Demand & Well-Being
affiliations: University of Bordeaux, IZA Institute of Labor Economics, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Gone with the Wind? Climate Shocks, Insurance Demand & Well-Being
detail.abstract: We study the medium-run effects of a major climate shock on insurance demand and subjective well-being. Exploiting quasi-random exposure to storm Gudrun (Sweden, 2005) and conditioning on satellite-based forest and terrain characteristics, we treat realized damages as conditionally exogenous. Three years after the event, affected forest owners exhibit a persistent increase in insurance take-up alongside significant welfare losses. These losses are economically meaningful and consistent with important non-pecuniary and psychological costs, including landscape damage and heightened insecurity. Insurance provides only limited welfare buffering, operating partly as reassurance rather than full compensation. Overall, the results highlight the limits of climate insurance as a stand-alone adaptation tool.

title: Sectoral Value Added and Employment Shifts as Drivers of Inclusive Growth in Sub Saharan Africa: Evidence from Structural Transformation Dynamics
affiliations: North-West University, Sol Plaatje University and North-West University

detail.title: Sectoral Value Added and Employment Shifts as Drivers of Inclusive Growth in Sub Saharan Africa: Evidence from Structural Transformation Dynamics
detail.abstract: The objective of this study is to investigate the linkage between structural transformation and inclusive growth in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) by empirically decoupling the different channels through which both sector value-added and cross-sector employment shifts operate. A compound measure of inclusive growth and structural transformation indices were developed to measure the multidimensional aspects of these dimensions. Based on unbalanced annual data from 2000 to 2024 of 32 SSA countries and using the Bias-Corrected Method of Moments (BC-MM) estimator; the results of this study have convincingly established a positive relationship between structural transformation and inclusive growth in SSA, indicating that broad-based sectoral reallocation is essential for shared prosperity. The twin-channel analysis shows that the shift of employment to the service sector is the most powerful and constant driver of inclusiveness, while manufacturing value-added has a statistically insignificant independent effect. This suggests that the form of transformation (including, in particular its ability to create productive employment) is more important than simply expanding some sectors. On the policy side, the results suggest that structural transformation in SSA should be pursued alongside policies that specifically aim to create jobs in high-absorbing sectors. Policy implications point to the need for structural transformation strategies that prioritize job creation in high-absorbing sectors, particularly services, alongside productivity-enhancing investments in agriculture. Strengthening domestic service sector capacity and improving the employment intensity of growth are critical for ensuring that structural transformation translates into inclusive and sustainable development in line with Africa’s Agenda 2063.

title: Electric Vehicle Charging at the Workplace Experimental Evidence on Incentives and Environmental Nudges
affiliations: University of Melbourne, School of Global Policy and Strategy, UCSD, University of California, San Diego (UCSD), University of California San Diego and UC San Diego, School of Global Policy and Strategy

detail.title: Electric Vehicle Charging at the Workplace Experimental Evidence on Incentives and Environmental Nudges
detail.abstract: Workplace charging is increasingly important for electric-vehicle (EV) adoption and for managing the grid impacts of transportation electrification, yet workplace networks operate under tight constraints: charging capacity is scarce, parking is bundled with chargers, and employers are reluctant to ask drivers to move vehicles during the workday. As a result, workplaces often rely on other policy tools (e.g., light-touch information and time-invariant price discounts) whose effects may differ from home or public charging settings. We study these policies in a natural field experiment with 629 EV drivers on a large university campus charging network. We randomize (i) informational emails emphasizing the environmental benefits of daytime charging and (ii) time-invariant discounts for workplace charging. Environmental nudges shift charging initiation modestly from early morning to later morning hours but do not increase total workplace charging. In contrast, price discounts increase total workplace charging but shift charging toward early-morning and evening periods when network utilization is lower. A followup experiment shows that perceived charger scarcity is a key mechanism shaping these timing responses, alongside congestion, charger reliability, and driver characteristics. We also translate the behavioral responses into illustrative emissions impacts and fiscal abatement costs.

title: Does gender diversity in boards affect corporate cash holdings? Evidence from global board gender diversity reforms
affiliations: City University of Hong Kong (CityU) - Department of Accountancy, Lingnan University and University of Sussex

detail.title: Does gender diversity in boards affect corporate cash holdings? Evidence from global board gender diversity reforms
detail.abstract: This study exploits the shock of global adoption of board gender diversity reforms (BGDRs) and examines their impacts on corporate cash holdings. While prior studies demonstrate improved corporate governance after the reforms, how corporate practices are shaped remains underexplored. We argue that cash holdings as an important corporate policy benefits from such improvement. Using a sample of firms from 42 countries, we find that BGDRs are associated with a significant reduction in cash holdings of about 7%. The negative effect is amplified for countries with imbalanced gender-related issues and weaker legal institutions, as well as for firms with more severe agency problems. We further demonstrate that firms are more likely to use cash for value-adding investing activities after the reforms and the reduced cash holdings contribute to higher firm value. Overall, our study supports for the value-creation proposition of gender diversity in boards through the lens of corporate cash policy.

title: Blowing the Roof Off: Extreme Storms and Operational Losses in the U.S. Banking Sector
affiliations: University of South Carolina - Darla Moore School of Business, Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond - Quantitative Supervision & Research, Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond,  and Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia

detail.title: Blowing the Roof Off: Extreme Storms and Operational Losses in the U.S. Banking Sector
detail.abstract: Using confidential supervisory data from large U.S. bank holding companies (BHCs), we provide the first empirical evidence that operational losses incurred by BHCs escalate significantly during extreme storm events. These losses are primarily driven by external fraud, failures to meet client obligations, faulty business practices, damage to physical assets, and business disruption. Event study estimations corroborate our baseline findings. We further show that BHCs with past exposure to extreme storms reduce operational losses from future exposure to storms. Beyond direct operational losses, we find that severe storms disrupt BHCs’ branch networks, hindering their physical presence in affected areas. Our findings provide new evidence regarding banking organizations’ exposure to severe weather with implications for risk management and supervisory policy.

title: A structural model of capital buffer usability
affiliations: European Central Bank (ECB) and Deutsche Bundesbank

detail.title: A structural model of capital buffer usability
detail.abstract: Under which conditions do usability constraints for regulatory capital buffers emerge? To answer this question, we build a non-linear structural banking sector model with a minimum capital requirement that banks are not allowed to breach, and a capital buffer requirement (CBR) that banks can breach but if they do so potential stigma applies. We prove that even very low stigma costs induce large buffer usability constraints, i.e. when faced with losses banks will deleverage significantly to avoid that their capital ratio falls below the CBR. Our findings imply that non-releasble regulatory capital buffers are unlikely to fully achieve their macro stabilisation goal to support aggregate loan supply when the banking system faces losses.

title: Systemic Barriers and Innovation Pathways for Europe’s Circular Bioeconomy: Grassroots Stakeholder Insights from 43 Multi-Actor Workshops
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Universidade de Coimbra, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Ljubljana, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Shandong Agricultural University

detail.title: Systemic Barriers and Innovation Pathways for Europe’s Circular Bioeconomy: Grassroots Stakeholder Insights from 43 Multi-Actor Workshops
detail.abstract: The bioeconomy is a key pillar of the European Green Deal, yet its implementation remains constrained by entrenched linear value chains, fragmented logistics systems, and regulatory uncertainty. This paper examines how practitioners across Europe envision circular bioeconomy transitions, drawing on evidence from 43 harmonised multi-actor workshops conducted in 14 countries with 1,078 participants from primary production, processing industries, technology provision, public authorities, and civil society. Using a structured participatory canvas and comparative thematic analysis, we analyse how stakeholders redesign existing value chains, which innovation pathways they prioritise, and which barriers they encounter in practice. Across agriculture, forestry, aquatic systems and bio-based industries, stakeholders consistently shift the focus from expanding biomass production toward improving the use of existing residues and side-streams. Dominant innovation pathways include residue valorisation, nutrient and water recycling, integrated bioenergy systems, and emerging biomaterials. At the same time, four interlinked barrier domains recur across countries and sectors: high and uncertain costs, immature or inaccessible technologies, weak feedstock logistics and pre-treatment infrastructure, and misaligned or unclear regulatory frameworks—most notably around waste and by-product classification. By providing one of the most extensive cross-country, practitioner-led analyses of circular bioeconomy value chains to date, the study offers granular evidence on how regulatory ambiguity, infrastructure gaps and investment risk constrain implementation on the ground. The findings point to a policy agenda focused on regulatory clarification rather than deregulation, coordinated investment in residue aggregation and pre-treatment infrastructure, and applied context-sensitive research to support scalable circular bio-based solutions.

title: Mapping barriers and pathways for a just energy transition in Austria’s rental housing: A dynamic systems perspective
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Universität für Bodenkultur Wien (BOKU)

detail.title: Mapping barriers and pathways for a just energy transition in Austria’s rental housing: A dynamic systems perspective
detail.abstract: The rental housing sector presents unique challenges for achieving a socially just energy transition (JET), particularly in countries with high proportions of tenants and fragmented governance structures. This paper uses Austria as a case study to examine barriers and pathways for a JET in the rental housing sector using a Causal Loop Diagram (CLD) to synthesize tenant, landlord, and political dynamics. Framed by energy justice and JET, the analysis maps how distributional, procedural, and recognition dimensions shape transition feasibility and pace. The CLD identifies key reinforcing and balancing feedbacks: profit-driven renovation (R1) and subsidy-driven renovation (R2) as latent engines of structural change; and income-consumption and stabilization dynamics (B1, B2), net-zero pressure (B3), and subsidy-inequity (B4) as key constraints. We show why refurbishment uptake remains low despite substantial subsidies: execution vetoes (tenant consent, co-ownership voting), strict cost-recovery limits, fragmented governance, and subsidy designs that skey toward owner-occupied dwellings weaken endogenous drivers (R1, R2), and tighten fairness-sensitive constraints (B4). These dynamics explain persistent under-investment and stagnant progress relative to climate targets.Building on this diagnosis, we propose a JET-consistent policy package that: (i) strengthens incentives for landlords; (ii) aligns landlord-tenant incentives while protecting affordability; and (iii) deploys command-and-control instruments paired with targeted support for vulnerable actors. Together, these measures aim to activate self-reinforcing dynamics while mitigating the stabilizing effects of balancing feedback behaviors, fostering sustained and equitable decarbonization. While the analysis focuses on Austria, the insights are transferable to other countries facing similar challenges in decarbonizing their rental housing sectors.
